Using corpus-level perplexity patterns as benchmark representations is an interesting and potentially novel direction.
The empirical scope—32 open models and 88 reported benchmarks/subtasks—is ambitious, and the paper provides a reasonably clear high-level pipeline and model inventory.
The observation that raw performance correlations can be dominated by benchmark family and answer format is useful and motivates better benchmark-agreement methods.
weaknesses: The central evaluation is circular. Benchmark performance on the same 32 models is used to select each signature, and signature overlap is then measured on those same models and compared with performance overlap. Consequently, the reported structure may be an artifact of supervised fitting rather than independent evidence of shared capabilities. This also contradicts the suggestion that signatures avoid direct benchmark evaluation.

The feature-selection regime is statistically untenable without much stronger controls: roughly 16.9 million features are searched using only 32 observations, with about 338,000 candidates retained per benchmark. Greedy AIC does not correct for this enormous adaptive search, and the reported approximately 30 selected features nearly saturate a 32-sample regression. Algorithm 4 also initializes against infinity rather than an intercept-only model, guaranteeing at least one selected feature. Extreme correlations are expected under this multiple-testing regime and do not demonstrate sparsity.

The reported leave-one-model-out result is not described as nested feature selection. If screening and AIC selection were performed once using all 32 responses, the held-out labels leaked into feature construction and the MAE result is invalid. Even a nested analysis would need permutation controls, selection-stability results, family-held-out evaluation, and genuinely independent models; comparison only with a mean predictor is inadequate.

The signature-overlap statistic is not justified. The method discards the fitted regression coefficients and their signs, then averages selected perplexities even though positively and negatively associated features are both retained. The reference population used for within-model z-scoring is unspecified. Moreover, different model tokenizers make a whitespace piece and its final subtoken non-comparable across models.

The semantic baseline is seriously flawed: all questions are concatenated and then truncated to the embedding model's maximum length, so nearly all benchmark items are discarded and the result depends largely on the first few questions. The appendix samples only the larger benchmark, contradicting the main-text description that both sides are bootstrapped. Thus, the claim of superiority over semantic similarity is unsupported.

There is no validated ground truth for 'true overlap.' Broad task labels are treated as validation, while the mapping to the eight design functions and the maximum-clique threshold are not reported. Figure 5 further treats dependent benchmark pairs as independent Mann–Whitney observations and interprets a nonsignificant difference as evidence that bias was resolved; neither inference is warranted.

Major confounders are uncontrolled, including parameter count, pretraining corpus, base versus instruction tuning, tokenizer, and repeated variants from the same model families. These factors can drive both perplexity and benchmark performance. No residualized, matched, mixed-effects, or model-family-held-out analysis is provided.

The claimed SIS justification is largely asserted. A peaked empirical correlation histogram and a fixed quantile selection rule do not establish sparsity, minimum signal strength, independence, or the sure-screening property—especially for highly related, non-i.i.d. model observations.

The experimental record is insufficient for reproduction and robustness assessment: code and selected signatures are absent; prompts, chat templates, decoding and few-shot settings, checkpoint revisions, random seeds, and exact functional labels are unspecified; and there are no ablations over corpus samples, thresholds, context length, selection method, or model subsets. The corpus accounting is also internally inconsistent: 8.45×10^9 contexts divided by 50 is 1.69×10^8, not the reported 1.69×10^7.

Claims of mechanistic insight, capacity familiarity, benchmark validity, and separation of competence from performance substantially exceed the correlational evidence. Addressing the circularity and overfitting would require a redesigned evaluation with independently held-out model families and external overlap criteria, not a minor revision.

Each benchmark has only 32 model observations, while screening starts from 16.9 million features, retains roughly 338,000, and then uses adaptive AIC selection to choose about 30 predictors—nearly saturating a regression with 32 samples. Extreme correlations are inevitable under this multiple-testing regime, even for random features. No null simulation, multiplicity control, random-feature baseline, or stability analysis is provided.

The reported leave-one-model-out result does not state that correlation screening and feature selection are rerun inside every fold; the described procedure appears to select signatures using all 32 outcomes and only refit the final regression after holding out a model. Independent held-out models are required to establish that the heatmaps are not selection artifacts.

Token perplexities are not directly comparable across the highly heterogeneous tokenizers in the model set. A whitespace piece can correspond to different subword sequences, yet the method records only the last token's perplexity. The analysis also fails to control for parameter count, model family, instruction tuning, release generation, or generic corpus perplexity, all of which can jointly drive both benchmark accuracy and token loss. Thus the signatures cannot presently be interpreted as training exposure or specific capability familiarity.

There is no defensible ground truth or external validation for benchmark overlap. The claim that signatures are 'better' is based mainly on greater heatmap variation and agreement with broad, partly undocumented category assignments. There are no held-out expert labels, retrieval or clustering metrics, predictive tests on new benchmarks, or comparisons with strong alternatives such as item-embedding aggregation, IRT/general-factor residualization, response-profile methods, or average-loss/PCA baselines.

The semantic comparison is an especially weak baseline: questions are concatenated and then truncated to the embedding model's maximum length, so most benchmark items are discarded and dataset order can dominate the result. The main text says both benchmarks are bootstrapped, whereas Appendix Algorithm 3 fixes the smaller benchmark and samples only the larger one. Consequently, the narrow semantic-similarity range does not substantiate the claimed superiority of signatures.

Several statistical claims are unsupported. A peaked marginal-correlation distribution is expected under a null and does not demonstrate sparsity; the paper only asserts rather than verifies the conditions needed for Sure Independence Screening. Pairwise benchmark correlations are dependent, making an ordinary Mann–Whitney test questionable, and failure to reject a difference is treated as evidence that bias has been removed. Error bars and the reported 'effect' in Figure 5 are not defined.

Important procedural details are ambiguous or internally inconsistent: z-scoring 'within the model' lacks a reference population; the design-function mapping is omitted; 8.45×10^9 divided by 50 is 1.69×10^8 rather than the reported 1.69×10^7; the listed MMLU and BBH entries already appear to total 88 although MBPP and IFEval are also analyzed; and the stated interpretation of the Pre-select coefficient has the opposite direction from its formula. No code, selected signatures, random seeds, or complete evaluation configuration is released.

Perplexity is correlational and reflects architecture, tokenization, scale, calibration, and post-training—not simply exposure or acquired capacity. Without controlled-model experiments or causal interventions, claims of 'mechanistic insights,' approximation of 'true overlap,' and conclusions about benchmark validity or LLM generalization substantially exceed the evidence. Addressing the core issues would require a redesigned, nested, out-of-sample evaluation rather than a minor revision.

weaknesses: The central statistical procedure is severely overfit. For each benchmark, roughly 338,000 candidates are retained from 16.9 million features, after which stepwise AIC selects about 30 predictors from only 32 model observations. With an intercept, this leaves roughly one residual degree of freedom. Ordinary AIC does not account for this enormous adaptive search and will favor near-interpolating models; no permutation-label control, selective-inference correction, or signature-stability analysis is provided. Consequently, the extracted signatures and downstream overlap claims are not reliable.

The stated LOOCV does not clarify whether screening and feature selection are rerun entirely within every fold. Global selection would leak the held-out outcome. Even a properly nested model-level LOOCV is inadequate here because many observations are related size variants from the same model families. There is no independent model test set or leave-one-family-out evaluation, and only aggregate MAE against a weak mean baseline is reported without uncertainty or per-benchmark results.

The signature-overlap statistic is insufficiently defined. The reference population used for within-model z-scoring is unspecified; z-scoring within each signature would make its mean degenerate. Moreover, overlap averages selected perplexities while discarding the fitted coefficients and their signs, even though both positively and negatively correlated features are selected. The paper gives no derivation showing that this quantity measures shared capability.

Perplexity is interpreted too strongly as training exposure or capacity. Cross-model perplexities are confounded by scale, architecture, tokenizer, base-versus-instruction tuning, and corpus composition. Because a whitespace piece may map to different subword targets across tokenizers, even the recorded last-token probabilities need not be directly comparable. No controls for parameter count, general benchmark ability, model family, tokenizer, or average corpus perplexity are included.

There is no credible ground truth demonstrating that the proposed matrix represents benchmark overlap. Coarse task categories are treated as truth without publishing the category-to-task mapping, while conclusions are inferred post hoc from heatmaps. Controlled synthetic benchmarks, expert overlap judgments, known duplicated-capability tasks, random-feature baselines, and comparisons with factor-analysis or residualized-performance methods are absent.

The semantic baseline is structurally weak: it concatenates an entire benchmark and truncates it to MPNet's maximum input length, so most questions are discarded and results can depend on ordering. Section 2 says both benchmarks are bootstrapped, whereas Algorithm 3 fixes the smaller benchmark and samples only the larger one. Its poor discrimination therefore does not establish superiority over sound semantic-overlap methods.

The inferential analysis treats many pairwise benchmark correlations sharing the same tasks as independent observations in Mann–Whitney tests. Error bars and effect-size definitions are not explained, p-values are reported as 0.000, and there are no dependence-aware confidence intervals or multiplicity corrections.

The empirical scope and reproducibility do not support the broad claims: the 88 outputs are dominated by MMLU and BBH subtasks, with only isolated coding and instruction-following benchmarks and no convincing multilingual evaluation. Actual signature contexts, code, sampled corpus identifiers, seeds, and complete evaluation settings are missing. The data accounting is also inconsistent: 8.45×10^9 contexts downsampled by 1/50 would yield 1.69×10^8, not the reported 1.69×10^7. These issues, together with the invalid high-dimensional validation, leave the central claims unsupported.

strengths: The paper addresses an important problem: determining whether proliferating LLM benchmarks measure distinct capabilities. The proposed use of corpus perplexity as a benchmark representation is creative and potentially useful.
The empirical scope is ambitious, covering 32 models and 88 benchmark/subtask scores across several domains.

The manuscript is generally well organized, provides explicit algorithms, and lists the evaluated models and tasks. The comparison among semantic-, performance-, and signature-level relations is conceptually appealing.
The observation that benchmark-suite and question-format artifacts can dominate raw performance correlations is plausible and worth investigating.
weaknesses: The central evaluation is circular and severely prone to overfitting. For each benchmark, the method screens roughly 16.9 million features using performance on only 32 models, retains about 338,000 candidates, and forward-selects approximately 30 predictors—nearly saturating the sample size. AIC does not account for this enormous adaptive search. The resulting signatures and their overlaps are then evaluated on the same models and perplexities used for selection. The LOOCV description does not establish that screening and selection are rerun inside every fold, and it does not validate the main overlap heatmaps in any case. Permuted-label, random-signature, fully nested, and genuinely held-out model-family evaluations are essential.

Perplexity features are not comparable as constructed across the heterogeneous tokenizers of the 32 models. The final token of a whitespace-delimited piece can correspond to different subword strings under different tokenizers, while raw token perplexity also depends strongly on vocabulary and tokenization. Model size, family, base-versus-instruction tuning, and training data jointly confound both perplexity and benchmark performance, yet none is controlled. The signatures may therefore encode general scale or family effects rather than benchmark-specific capacity.

There is a mismatch between signature fitting and signature comparison: regression coefficients and correlation directions are discarded, and standardized perplexities for positively and negatively associated selected tokens are simply averaged. Such effects can cancel or be treated as equivalent, and no derivation or validation shows that the resulting Spearman correlation estimates shared capability.

The paper provides no credible ground truth for benchmark overlap. Better visual separation of author-assigned broad categories is not sufficient validation, especially without quantitative retrieval or classification metrics, uncertainty estimates, held-out categories, annotation reliability, or comparisons to stronger baselines such as residualized performance, item-level embeddings, random tokens, average corpus loss, model size, PCA, ridge, or lasso. The conclusions about coding being clean and cross-domain capability entanglement are consequently speculative.

The semantic baseline is materially flawed. It concatenates all questions and truncates the result to the encoder's maximum length, so only a small and order-dependent prefix represents a benchmark. The main text says both benchmarks are bootstrapped, whereas Algorithm 3 fixes the smaller benchmark and samples only the larger one. This invalidates the claim that semantic overlap is intrinsically less discriminative.

The statistical evidence is inadequate. Pairwise benchmark correlations are non-independent, yet ordinary Mann–Whitney tests appear to treat them as independent; thousands of correlations receive no uncertainty or multiplicity treatment; error bars and effect-size definitions are unspecified; and failure to reject differences at p=0.071 or p=0.805 is interpreted as evidence that bias has been 'resolved.' The maximum-clique threshold is also unspecified.

The SIS justification is largely asserted rather than demonstrated. With millions of features and 32 observations, extreme sample correlations occur under pure noise; a distribution centered near zero with thin tails does not establish sparsity or minimum signal strength. Moreover, the stated Pre-select formula gives its maximum—not zero—under the paper's own ideal ordering, and the Thrush statistic is described as counting concordant pairs although its formula weights pairs by rank differences.

Reproducibility is insufficient for the scale and sensitivity of the claims. The corpus accounting is inconsistent: 8.45×10^9 instances downsampled by 1/50 would yield 1.69×10^8, not 1.69×10^7, and a nominal 1B-token corpus cannot straightforwardly produce 8.45×10^9 one-per-piece contexts. Exact prompts, shot settings, decoding parameters, embedding checkpoint, seeds, software versions, category assignments, selected tokens, regression coefficients, and code are absent. Most of the claimed 88 benchmarks are also correlated subtasks from only MMLU and BBH rather than independent benchmark families.

Because these issues undermine the validity and interpretation of the signature-overlap matrices, the manuscript's central mechanistic and benchmark-design claims are not supported by the reported evidence.

The statistical analysis does not account for dependence among benchmark pairs, uncertainty from only 32 models, repeated comparisons, or post-selection effects such as maximum-clique extraction. Reported Mann-Whitney tests and statements that correlations such as 0.21 are significant are consequently unsupported.

Several reproducibility inconsistencies remain: a 1-billion-token source is said to yield 8.45 billion contexts, and downsampling 8.45 billion by 1/50 would yield 169 million rather than 16.9 million. The stated 88-task matrix is not clearly reconciled with the MMLU/BBH aggregates and the separately discussed MBPP and IFEval experiments. Code, selected signatures, score matrices, exact harness versions, and sampling seeds are not released.

Most analyzed units are correlated subtasks or aggregates from MMLU and BBH rather than 88 independent benchmark datasets, substantially narrowing the empirical scope. The observational results do not justify claims of mechanistic insight, training exposure, true capability overlap, or resolved evaluation bias. Addressing the problems would require a major redesign rather than a small revision.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and important problem: determining whether proliferating LLM benchmarks measure distinct capabilities.
The proposed use of in-the-wild perplexity patterns as benchmark signatures is creative and potentially useful.

The empirical effort is substantial, spanning 32 open models, many benchmark subfields, and three notions of overlap. The family/format effects observed in raw performance correlations are particularly interesting.
The pipeline is presented with algorithms, model lists, data sources, and generally clear visualizations.
weaknesses: The central estimation procedure is extremely vulnerable to overfitting: roughly 16.9 million features are screened using only 32 observations, hundreds of thousands survive screening, and forward AIC typically selects about 30 predictors—nearly saturating the sample. No null-feature experiment, multiplicity correction, or selection-stability analysis is provided. Moreover, the paper does not establish that screening and feature selection are rerun inside every leave-one-out fold; otherwise the reported MAE contains target leakage.

There is substantial circularity in the main validation. Tokens are selected for predicting benchmark scores on the 32 models, and signature overlap is then computed from those tokens on the same models. There is no genuinely independent model set, model-family holdout, second corpus, or controlled benchmark suite with known capability overlap. Consequently, the claimed mapping of latent capabilities and mechanistic interpretation are not established.

Both perplexity and benchmark performance are strongly confounded by model size, family, instruction tuning, and overall competence. These factors are not controlled. Per-token likelihoods are also not directly comparable across heterogeneous tokenizers, and within-model z-scoring does not resolve differences in token segmentation.

The semantic comparison is an unusually weak baseline: questions are concatenated and truncated to the encoder context window, so only a small, order-dependent portion of each benchmark is represented. The prose and Algorithm 3 also disagree about whether both benchmarks are bootstrapped. Stronger item-level distribution or matching methods are needed before concluding that semantic overlap is uninformative.

The statistical evidence is insufficient. Pairwise benchmark correlations are dependent, yet Mann–Whitney tests appear to treat them as independent; uncertainty intervals, multiple-testing corrections, effect-size definitions, and robustness across model subsets are absent. Failure to reject a difference is also interpreted as proof that family/format bias is “resolved,” without an equivalence test.

The scope and reproducibility do not support the breadth of the claims. Most measures are MMLU or BBH subfields, with very limited coding and instruction-following coverage; no actual learned signatures, code, seeds, or exact evaluation configurations are released. There are also internal inconsistencies, including the RedPajama counts: 8.45×10^9 divided by 50 is 1.69×10^8, not 1.69×10^7. Overall, the idea is promising, but the current evaluation does not validate the central claims at a top-tier standard.

strengths: The paper addresses an important problem: benchmark redundancy and construct validity are increasingly consequential as evaluation suites proliferate.

The proposed connection between benchmark behavior and perplexity on naturally occurring text is creative, and considering semantic-, performance-, and signature-level relationships is conceptually appealing.
The empirical scope is ambitious, covering 32 models, many benchmark subfields, and a large corpus; the paper also provides model/task lists and reasonably clear high-level algorithms.
The observation that benchmark-family and question-format effects can dominate raw performance correlations is useful and deserves rigorous follow-up.
weaknesses: The central procedure is statistically untenable. For each response vector containing only 32 models, the method screens 16.9 million features, retains roughly 338,000, and uses forward AIC selection to choose about 30 predictors. Including an intercept leaves roughly one residual degree of freedom. Searching such an enormous feature pool will find near-perfect chance correlates and nearly saturate arbitrary response vectors; AIC does not correct for this adaptive multiple testing.

The evaluation is circular: token features are selected using the benchmark scores of the same 32 models on which signature overlaps are subsequently computed. The LOOCV description does not establish that screening and feature selection are rerun entirely within every fold; selecting signatures before LOOCV would leak held-out outcomes. No genuinely unseen models or held-out model families validate the signatures.

Essential null controls are absent. There are no label-permutation experiments, random-token signatures, corpus-resampling stability analyses, or comparisons against simple controls such as model size, global perplexity, tokenizer identity, or principal components of model performance. With millions of tests, thin correlation tails are expected under the null and do not demonstrate sparsity.

Perplexities are not directly comparable across the heterogeneous models used. The models have different tokenizers and vocabularies, so the last subword token associated with a whitespace-delimited piece is not a consistent prediction event. Model scale, training corpus, architecture, instruction tuning, and tokenizer family can jointly confound both perplexity and benchmark performance. The underspecified within-model z-scoring step does not resolve the raw-feature selection confound.

The signature-overlap calculation discards the fitted regression coefficients and their signs, despite screening both positively and negatively correlated tokens. Averaging all selected perplexities equally therefore has no principled connection to the predictive regression used to define a signature.

The semantic comparison is a weak and potentially invalid baseline: questions are concatenated and then truncated to MPNet's maximum length, meaning only a small, order-dependent fraction of a benchmark may determine its representation. Section 2 and Algorithm 3 also disagree about whether both benchmarks or only the larger one are resampled.

The statistical analysis of family/format effects is insufficient. Pairwise correlations sharing benchmarks are treated as independent observations in Mann-Whitney tests, and failure to reject differences at p=0.071 or p=0.805 is interpreted as evidence that bias has been resolved rather than as absence of evidence. Sample counts, dependence-aware uncertainty, equivalence tests, and multiple-comparison handling are missing.

The cited sure-independence-screening theory does not justify the implemented pipeline. Its assumptions are asserted qualitatively rather than verified, the rank-based fixed-quantile screen is not shown to inherit the claimed guarantee, and the appendix's statement that log(d)>m is numerically false for either reported d with m=32.

There is no independent ground truth for benchmark overlap, and the paper makes causal or mechanistic claims—such as signatures reflecting true capacities, coding benchmarks being cleaner, or logic benchmarks measuring instruction following—from correlations that cannot distinguish ability, contamination, overall model quality, or training exposure. No selected token contexts are shown to support the proposed interpretations.

Reproducibility is inadequate for the scale and sensitivity of the analysis: code and derived signatures are not provided, and important details such as data version and sampling seed, model revisions, evaluation prompts/configurations, exact normalization reference, regression implementation, and feature-selection stability are missing. The reported 1B-token corpus is also inconsistent with an initial pool of 8.45 billion token contexts, and the evaluation description does not cover all 88 claimed targets.

strengths: The paper addresses an important meta-evaluation problem: determining whether apparently different LLM benchmarks measure overlapping capabilities.

Using perplexity on naturally occurring text as a benchmark fingerprint is a creative idea, and the three-way comparison among semantic, performance, and signature-level overlap is conceptually appealing.

The empirical scope is computationally ambitious, covering 32 identified open models and numerous tasks or subfields. The observation that benchmark family and answer format strongly influence performance correlations is potentially useful.
The manuscript provides high-level algorithms, a model inventory, and limited checks involving leave-one-out prediction and perplexity granularity.
weaknesses: The central evaluation in the reviewed manuscript :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/r-3b30f255031c4d37/reviews/review-experiment-ael93j_e/call-e656f6b7a4fc487181e7689f3b903dc0/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"} is circular. Each signature is selected to predict a benchmark's performance over the same 32 models on which signature overlap is subsequently computed. Consequently, the overlap matrix is an adaptively constructed transformation of the original performance data, not independent evidence that perplexity reveals underlying capabilities or removes performance-level biases.

The feature-selection regime is statistically untenable without strong null controls: approximately 16.9 million token features are screened using only 32 observations, roughly 338,000 extreme features are retained, and forward AIC search selects about 30 predictors. Extreme correlations and near-saturated fits are inevitable under the null after this degree of multiple testing. There are no label-permutation experiments, false-discovery control, random-token baselines, stability-selection results, or selection-adjusted inference.

The leave-one-out result does not state that token screening and AIC selection are repeated entirely within every training fold. If the reported signatures were selected using all 32 models, the held-out targets leaked into feature selection. Even a properly nested model-wise split would be weak because many observations are closely related variants from the same model families; evaluation should hold out complete families and an independent set of models.

Major confounders are uncontrolled. Model size, training compute, age, instruction tuning, architecture, tokenizer, family, and average corpus loss all affect both benchmark performance and token perplexity. The signatures may therefore encode generic model strength or family/training-corpus identity rather than benchmark-specific capacity. No residualization or comparison against these simple baselines is provided.

Perplexities are not directly comparable across the heterogeneous tokenizers used by the 32 models. A whitespace-delimited target may correspond to different subword sequences, making 'last-token perplexity' a different event for different models. Within-model z-scoring does not resolve this, and the population used to compute those z-scores is not specified.

The signature aggregation is not justified. Screening deliberately retains both positively and negatively associated tokens, and the regression may assign coefficients of either sign, yet overlap is computed from an unweighted mean of token z-scores rather than coefficient-oriented predictions. Opposing signals can cancel, and the resulting correlation has no demonstrated relationship to shared capability.

There is no construct validation for the proposed overlap measure. The paper does not test duplicated benchmarks, controlled mixtures, shared-item variants, or other cases with known overlap. Nor does it show the selected contexts, their semantic coherence, selection stability across corpus samples, or robustness to hyperparameters and alternative corpora. Calling the result 'mechanistic' is unsupported by this correlational analysis.

The semantic comparator is seriously flawed: all questions are concatenated and then truncated to the embedding model's maximum length, so most questions are discarded and the score can depend on arbitrary ordering. Moreover, the main-text description bootstraps both benchmarks, whereas Algorithm 3 fixes the smaller benchmark and samples only the larger one. This weak comparator cannot substantiate claims of superior discrimination.

The statistical analysis of Figure 5 treats overlapping benchmark pairs as independent Mann-Whitney observations, although many pairs share the same benchmark. Its p-values are therefore not valid under the stated test. More generally, failure to find a significant difference is not evidence that family or format bias has been 'resolved'; this would require a powered equivalence test. Confidence intervals, multiple-comparison handling, and the threshold used for the reported maximum clique are also absent.

The claimed breadth is overstated: most columns are subdomains of only MMLU and BBH rather than independent benchmark designs, while coding and instruction following appear to be represented by single benchmarks. Dataset accounting is also unclear: Table 2 already enumerates 60 MMLU and 28 BBH entries, totaling the stated 88, while MBPP and IFEval are additionally described as included.

The Sure Independence Screening discussion does not establish the theorem's required signal and covariance conditions, nor show that its guarantees transfer to the paper's rank statistic and dependent model sample. A peaked empirical correlation distribution with tails is not evidence of sparsity when millions of null features are searched. Likewise, token-level granularity is chosen because it has larger correlation dispersion, which can indicate noise and overfitting rather than predictive signal.

Reproducibility is inadequate for the central claims: no code, sampled corpus identifiers, learned signatures, performance matrix, model revisions, prompts, decoding settings, random seeds, or complete normalization procedure are supplied. The statement that a '1B-token' corpus produces 8.45 billion target contexts is also unexplained. Finally, the claim that signatures avoid direct benchmark evaluation contradicts Algorithm 1, which requires benchmark performance labels from every model used to construct them.

strengths: Addresses an important meta-evaluation question and proposes an original idea: characterizing benchmark relationships through corpus-level perplexity profiles.
The empirical scope is broad, covering 32 models, many model families, and 89 benchmark/subtask entries across diverse domains.
The paper attempts unusually extensive robustness analyses, including alternative selection methods, corpora, thresholds, corpus scales, and held-out-model prediction.
Algorithms, model and benchmark lists, computational costs, qualitative examples, and ethics/LLM-use disclosures are provided.
weaknesses: The central analysis is critically vulnerable to adaptive overfitting: millions of token features are screened against only 32 outcomes, followed by stepwise AIC selection of roughly 30 features. This nearly saturates the regression, while ordinary AIC is not valid protection against multiple testing and post-selection bias in this p≫n regime. The reported overlap matrices are then computed on the same models used to select the signatures.

The validation does not repair this problem. It is unclear whether feature selection is nested inside every LOOCV fold; two fully held-out models cannot validate correlations across models; the held-out models share families with training models; and the cross-task comparison contrasts features selected for different targets, making low task-specific training error expected. Strong baselines based on model size, family, mean corpus loss, or general benchmark ability are absent.

The signature-overlap statistic is underdefined and discards important information. The reference population for within-model z-scoring is unspecified, and selected features with positive and negative regression coefficients are averaged without their signs or weights. Moreover, different model tokenizers assign different final subtokens and vocabularies to a whitespace-delimited context, making token perplexities across models poorly comparable.

The semantic baseline is not credible: entire benchmark question sets are concatenated and then truncated to the encoder limit, so most items contribute nothing. The formal definition samples both benchmarks, whereas Algorithm 3 fixes the smaller set and samples only the larger one. Consequently, the claimed superiority over semantic overlap is not established.

Key confounds remain uncontrolled. Model size, lineage, instruction tuning, and general capability can drive both perplexity and performance. The format comparison is also largely confounded with benchmark family because the multiple-choice group is MMLU while the true/false group is BBH. Pairwise tests treat dependent correlations as observations, lack hierarchical resampling or multiplicity correction, and rely on uneven or apparently singleton functional categories.

The interpretation substantially exceeds the evidence. No controlled benchmarks with known overlaps, synthetic mixtures, causal interventions, or corpus decontamination validate that signatures recover capability overlap. RedPajama may contain benchmark-related material, and semantically implausible examples such as the coding signature centered on “evil” are at least as consistent with extreme-value feature selection as with a distinct model conceptual structure.

Several robustness checks are methodologically weak: Lasso and Elastic Net use arbitrary fixed penalties without reported standardization or cross-validation; mutual information is judged by score dispersion rather than predictive validity; nested threshold sets make later stability unsurprising; and RedPajama and Dolma share major source domains.

Reproducibility is insufficient despite the stated claim: the promised code/data link is missing, and exact embedding checkpoint, normalization procedure, prompts, evaluation settings, software versions, and seeds are not reported. There are also material numerical inconsistencies: 8.45×10^9 divided by 50 is 1.69×10^8, not 1.69×10^7, and the stated feature-pool dimensions conflict across sections. These issues collectively leave the main empirical claims unsupported.

Regression coefficients—including their signs—are discarded, and each signature is represented by an unweighted mean of selected perplexities. Because both positively and negatively associated features are admitted, that mean need not predict the benchmark at all. The population used for within-model z-scoring is also unspecified, and different model tokenizers may assign the purported target token to different subtokens.

The semantic baseline is invalid as implemented: all questions are concatenated and then truncated to the encoder's maximum length, so only a small, order-dependent fraction of a benchmark can determine its embedding. Algorithm 3 fixes the smaller benchmark and samples only the larger one, contradicting the main-text description that both are bootstrapped. Consequently, the claimed superiority over semantic overlap is not informative.

The performance baseline is not controlled for model scale, family, instruction tuning, release generation, or general capability. The model panel contains many closely related variants and mixes base and instruction-tuned models. These factors plausibly drive both perplexity and benchmark scores, yet no residualization, factor-analysis baseline, or leave-family-out validation is performed.

There is no independent ground truth for “true” benchmark overlap. Matching broad human-assigned categories, or eliminating a family/format effect, does not establish that signatures recover latent capabilities; format itself can impose genuine shared competence demands. Claims about capability entanglement, benchmark leakage, generalization, and benchmark validity therefore substantially exceed the correlational evidence.

The inferential analysis treats many pairwise benchmark correlations as though they were independent even though each benchmark appears in numerous pairs. The bootstrap and Mann–Whitney procedures are insufficiently specified, percentage effects and error bars are unclear, p-values are reported as 0.00, and no multiple-testing correction is given. Broad conclusions about coding and instruction following also appear to rely on only one benchmark per function.

Benchmark contamination is not addressed. RedPajama can contain benchmark items or close derivatives, but there is no deduplication or overlap audit. Agreement with Dolma mainly demonstrates stability across two substantially overlapping web-data mixtures, not that the signatures measure capability rather than contamination or shared training exposure.

Reproducibility is poor and internally inconsistent: a purported 1B-token corpus allegedly yields 8.45 billion contexts; dividing that value by 50 does not produce the reported 16.9 million instances; pre- and post-filter feature counts conflict; selecting both 1% tails retains 2%, not 1%; and the 32-model setup conflicts with a later reference to 27 training models. Complexity claims are also inconsistent. As submitted, the paper provides no working repository link, raw matrices, complete signatures, exact evaluation configurations, or seeds, and the abstract's open-source sentence is unfinished.

The robustness studies do not resolve these issues: random features are sampled only after outcome-dependent screening, regularizer hyperparameters are not meaningfully tuned, nested candidate sets make high threshold-to-threshold agreement partly automatic, and the cross-task comparison contrasts a likely saturated task-specific fit with a mismatched transfer setting. These experiments test stability more than validity.

The empirical effort is ambitious, covering 32 models, many benchmark sub-tasks, large corpora, and two corpus sources.
The authors attempt several robustness analyses, including held-out models, alternative selection procedures, threshold sensitivity, corpus sensitivity, and computational-cost reporting.

weaknesses: The central statistical procedure is fundamentally vulnerable to spurious discovery: only 32 observations are used to screen millions of features with the target labels and then perform greedy AIC selection, typically retaining about 30 predictors. This nearly saturated regression does not account for the enormous preceding search. A peaked marginal-correlation distribution is expected under a null and does not establish sparsity or the unverified SIS conditions. Label permutations, stability selection, and fully nested validation of the entire pipeline are essential.

The evaluation is circular: signatures are selected to predict benchmark scores across the same models whose perplexities are then used to define signature overlap. The resulting structure can inherit benchmark-performance correlations or generic model quality, family, scale, and training-data effects. The cross-task experiment does not residualize these confounds, while the two-model holdout uses only a mean baseline, has unexplained training-set counts, and evaluates prediction rather than validity of the claimed overlap structure.

Token-level perplexities are not made comparable across heterogeneous tokenizers. A whitespace-delimited target can map to different subtoken sequences, yet the method records only the final token probability. Rank transformations do not repair differences in target identity or segmentation, and the reference population used for within-model z-scoring is unspecified.

The semantic baseline is technically unsound: it concatenates an entire benchmark and truncates it to the encoder limit, so most questions are discarded. Moreover, the main text says both benchmarks are bootstrapped, whereas Algorithm 3 fixes the smaller benchmark and samples only the larger. Consequently, the claimed superiority over semantic overlap is not informative.

The statistical analysis treats overlapping benchmark pairs as if they supplied independent evidence, gives an unclear bootstrap procedure, reports p-values as 0.00, and provides no multiple-testing correction. Benchmark family, question format, and subject are heavily confounded, so the paper cannot conclude that signatures specifically remove format or family bias.

The 89 targets are dominated by correlated MMLU and BBH sub-tasks rather than independent benchmark suites. Comparisons omit strong alternatives such as factor analysis or IRT, partial correlations controlling for global ability and model family, average-corpus-loss baselines, and random-label or random-token controls.

There are serious reproducibility inconsistencies. For example, downsampling 8.45×10^9 contexts by 1/50 gives 1.69×10^8, not the reported 1.69×10^7; feature counts across sections do not reconcile; the complexity discussion does not match the stated exhaustive forward-selection algorithm; and the promised code/data link is absent, leaving the abstract sentence incomplete.

The evidence is associative, but the conclusions invoke training exposure, underlying capacity demands, true benchmark overlap, bias resolution, and claims such as coding being comparatively clean. The qualitative signatures—including a literary token for coding—could instead be artifacts of extreme feature search. Thus, the central interpretive claims are unsupported by the current design.

strengths: The paper targets an important and timely problem: identifying redundancy and capability overlap among increasingly numerous LLM benchmarks.

The proposed three-level comparison—semantic, performance, and perplexity-based signatures—is conceptually interesting, and the observation that benchmark family and response format can confound performance correlations is potentially useful.
The empirical scope is ambitious, covering many benchmarks, 32 models, and large web corpora, with several attempted robustness analyses and generally clear visual presentation.
weaknesses: The central signature-overlap statistic is not technically justified. Tokens are selected using benchmark performance on the same 32 models on which overlap is subsequently measured, creating severe double-dipping. More importantly, the overlap calculation averages selected perplexities while discarding the fitted regression coefficients and their signs; it therefore does not faithfully represent the predictive regression from which the signature was obtained.

The feature-selection regime is extremely prone to spurious discovery: millions of candidates are screened against only 32 observations, followed by uncorrected forward AIC selection of roughly 30 predictors on the same data. This nearly saturated regression, combined with massive multiple testing, can fit noise almost arbitrarily well. There is no permutation null, false-discovery control, nested validation, or sufficiently large independent model panel.

The claimed SIS justification is largely asserted rather than established. Its independence, signal-strength, and covariance assumptions are not tested, and the paper's statement that log(d) > m is numerically false for the reported d and m. A peaked null-like distribution of marginal correlations does not provide evidence of sparsity, especially when tail features are selected by construction.

The reported validation does not resolve leakage. It is unclear whether screening and AIC selection are rerun inside every LOOCV fold. The additional holdout contains only two models and inconsistently refers to 27 training models despite the main study using 32. The cross-task experiment is also insufficiently specified and appears internally inconsistent: an in-sample OLS fit with an intercept cannot have greater error than the mean-only fit, yet the paper reports exactly this outcome.

Major model-level confounds are uncontrolled. The model panel contains related checkpoints from the same families, widely varying parameter counts, and a mixture of base, chat, and instruction-tuned models. Model size, family, tokenizer, and post-training can drive both perplexity and benchmark scores. Moreover, the last subtoken's perplexity is compared across incompatible tokenizers rather than using a consistent word-level likelihood. Z-scoring does not eliminate these confounds.

The semantic baseline is invalid as a benchmark-level comparison: all questions are concatenated and then truncated to MPNet's context limit, so the representation can depend on only a small, order-dependent prefix of each benchmark. Consequently, the claim that signatures distinguish benchmarks better than semantic methods is not supported by a credible baseline.

The statistical analysis treats many shared-benchmark pairs as though they were independent, reports p-values as 0.00 without confidence intervals, and provides no external ground truth for what constitutes true capability overlap. Several broad conclusions—especially those about coding, instruction following, and missing-information detection—are effectively based on a single benchmark per function.

The robustness studies mostly measure agreement among variants that share the same response-leaking prefilter, rather than correctness. Stability across thresholds, regularizers, or two overlapping web corpora cannot establish construct validity. The qualitative interpretation is based on a handful of selected examples without systematic annotation, uncertainty estimates, or quantitative evidence.

There are substantial reproducibility and consistency problems: a 1B-token corpus is said to yield 8.45 billion contexts; dividing 8.45 billion by 50 is incorrectly reported as 16.9 million; top-and-bottom 1% filtering is described inconsistently; complexity claims conflict across sections; and the promised code/data link is missing. Exact prompts, decoding settings, model revisions, tokenizer treatment, and random seeds are also not provided.

Because these issues undermine both the construction of the signatures and the evidence that they measure benchmark capability overlap, the paper's main conclusions about benchmark validity and an underlying LLM capacity space are unsupported. Addressing them would require a substantially redesigned, nested out-of-sample evaluation with independent model families and validated overlap criteria.

Millions of features are screened against only 32 observations using the same benchmark outcomes later used for stepwise AIC selection. Selecting roughly 30 predictors nearly saturates the regression. AIC does not correct for the preceding massive search, and the observed correlation tails are expected under multiple testing rather than evidence of sparsity. No label-permutation null or genuinely nested evaluation validates the reported signature matrices.

The proposed overlap measure is not justified by the regression. It averages selected perplexity features without using their fitted coefficients or accounting for coefficient signs, despite signatures containing both positively and negatively associated tokens. The normalization reference is also unclear. Consequently, the resulting correlation need not represent either predicted performance or shared capability demands.

Token-level perplexities are not comparable as implemented across heterogeneous tokenizers. Recording only the final model token of a whitespace-delimited target can measure different subword strings for different models. Model scale, lineage, vocabulary, training corpus, and instruction tuning remain major uncontrolled common causes of both perplexity and benchmark performance.

The validation does not rescue the central claims. It is unclear whether feature selection is rerun inside every LOOCV fold; the stricter experiment uses only two held-out models, apparently related to training model families, only BBH tasks, and a weak mean baseline. Most importantly, the benchmark-overlap matrices themselves are not reconstructed and evaluated entirely on held-out model families.

The statistical tests treat pairwise matrix entries sharing benchmarks as if they were independent, making the bootstrap and Mann-Whitney p-values potentially anti-conservative. There is no multiple-testing correction or adequate uncertainty analysis. Family and question format are also strongly confounded—most MMLU tasks are multiple choice—so the claim that signatures resolve format bias is not identified by the experiment.

The comparison baselines are inadequate. The semantic baseline concatenates questions beyond MPNet's context limit and truncates them; its description is inconsistent between the main text and appendix and is asymmetric in the appendix. There are no competitive factor-analysis, IRT, residualized-performance, model-size/global-perplexity, task-representation, or full-pipeline random-label baselines.

There is no independent ground truth establishing that greater agreement with coarse author-assigned categories means a better measure of benchmark overlap. Claims about coding being clean, benchmark validity, generalization limitations, and an interconnected capacity space are therefore substantially stronger than the evidence. The qualitative analysis consists largely of selected examples without systematic evaluation or controls.
